paras: If you ask a vendor why a deal was won, you will usually hear about the product. If you ask the buyer, you will hear about something else entirely. In enterprise software the decision is almost never made in the room where the demo happens. It is made afterwards, by three or four people who were not in that room, and who are asking a question the demo did not answer: what happens to us if this goes wrong.

That is why the pitches that cut through the noise are rarely the most impressive ones. If a supplier only shows what the system does when everything works, the buyer has to imagine the rest, and what people imagine is always worse than the truth. The pitches that win tend to do the opposite. They start from the risk: they explain the data migration before anybody asks, they show the audit trail, they say out loud how long onboarding takes and how many people it needs. If companies do not know what deployment will cost them in hours, they assume the worst, and the worst is what they budget for.

There is a second thing buyers do that vendors consistently underestimate. They talk to each other. A proof of concept that goes badly at one company is discussed at three others within a month, and no amount of marketing survives that conversation. Which is the argument for being conservative about what you promise: if you say the integration will take eight weeks and it takes twelve, you have not lost eight weeks. You have lost the reference. The bottom line is that reducing the buyer's exposure is worth more than adding a feature, and it is a great deal cheaper to do.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: If you automate the filing, your team will save about two weeks a quarter.
If the migration starts in October, we will be live before your fiscal year ends.
If companies do not keep an audit trail, they cannot prove anything afterwards.
If you have any concerns about deployment, I will walk you through it now.
What this means for you is less exposure, not more features.
If we say eight weeks, it will be eight weeks. That is why I am saying twelve.

listenings.text: I sat through about forty vendor pitches last year and I can tell you exactly what happens. Somebody spends thirty minutes showing me a system doing everything perfectly, and the whole time I am sitting there thinking about the two weeks in January when nothing works and my team is doing it by hand. Nobody ever talks about that part. If a supplier opens with the migration, if they tell me before I ask how long onboarding really takes with four hundred users, my whole posture changes. That is the one that gets the second meeting. And here is the thing that vendors never seem to believe: I am not looking for the best product. I have a perfectly adequate product right now. I am looking for the one that will not become my problem in February.

We lost a deal two years ago for a reason I still think about. Everything went well, the proof of concept worked, the numbers were good, and then in the last meeting somebody asked how long the deployment would take, and my colleague said eight weeks. It was not a lie. It was optimistic. And the buyer had already called two of our clients, and both of them had told him it took about four months. So the number was not the problem. The problem was that we had said something he could check, and it did not match. If you are ever unsure, give the longer number. Nobody has ever cancelled a contract because a project finished early, and I have never once regretted saying twelve when I thought it might be eight.
